questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing taxonomy with systematics and the biological species concept with identification by morphology alone
questions.question: A student says: "Taxonomy and systematics mean exactly the same thing, and two populations that look alike must belong to one species." Which comparison corrects the student?
options: A) Taxonomy deals only with naming, while systematics deals only with collecting specimens; a species is any group living in one place
B) Systematics is the study of fossils alone; species are recognised only by the shape of their leaves or bones

C) Taxonomy covers characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification of organisms, whereas systematics is broader and also takes account of evolutionary relationships between organisms; a species is a group of individuals with fundamental similarities, and populations that interbreed freely in nature to produce fertile offspring belong to one species even if they differ in appearance, while look-alike populations that are reproductively isolated are different species
D) Taxonomy and systematics are identical; two populations that cannot interbreed must belong to the same genus and the same species
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Systematics adds evolutionary relationships to taxonomy, and a species is defined by fundamental similarity and natural interbreeding, not by looks alone.
Concept: Characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification are the processes basic to taxonomy. The word systematics comes from the Latin "systema", meaning systematic arrangement; Linnaeus used Systema Naturae as the title of his publication. The scope of systematics was later enlarged to include identification, nomenclature and classification, and systematics takes into account evolutionary relationships between organisms. Taxonomic studies treat a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities as a species. One can distinguish one species from a closely related species on the basis of distinct morphological differences, but under the biological species concept the decisive test is whether populations interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring.
Why: Appearance can mislead in both directions. Breeds of dogs look very different yet interbreed, so they are one species; some sibling species look almost identical but do not interbreed, so they are separate species.
Why not the others: (A) Taxonomy is more than naming, and systematics is not specimen collecting; species are not defined by locality. (B) Systematics is not limited to fossils, and morphology is not the only criterion. (D) The two terms differ in scope, and reproductive isolation marks different species.
Key point: Systematics = taxonomy + evolutionary relationships; species = interbreeding, fertile populations with fundamental similarities.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing schizocoelous and enterocoelous coelom formation and the change from bilateral larvae to radial adults in echinoderms
questions.question: Animals P (earthworm), Q (cockroach), R (starfish) and S (fish) are all triploblastic and coelomate. Which comparison of P–S is correct?
options: A) In P and Q the coelom forms by splitting of the mesoderm (schizocoelom) and the blastopore becomes the mouth (protostomes), whereas in R and S the coelom forms from pouches of the archenteron (enterocoelom) and the blastopore becomes the anus (deuterostomes); R has bilaterally symmetrical larvae but radially symmetrical adults, while S is bilateral throughout
B) All four are enterocoelous, and all four have radially symmetrical adults
C) P and R are pseudocoelomates, Q and S are acoelomates
D) R is diploblastic like a jellyfish because its adult is radially symmetrical
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Annelids and arthropods are schizocoelous protostomes; echinoderms and chordates are enterocoelous deuterostomes; starfish larvae are bilateral, adults radial.
Concept: Animals in which the body cavity is lined by mesoderm are coelomates; annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates are coelomates. Animals in which the cells are arranged in three embryonic layers are triploblastic. Echinoderm adults are radially symmetrical, but their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical, which links them with other bilateral triploblastic groups. In protostomes the coelom typically arises as a split in the mesoderm (schizocoelom); in deuterostomes (echinoderms, hemichordates, chordates) it arises from outpocketings of the primitive gut (enterocoelom).
Why: Germ layers and the mode of coelom formation are fixed early in development and are more reliable indicators of relationship than adult symmetry, which in echinoderms is a secondary adaptation to a slow-moving, bottom-dwelling life.
Why not the others: (B) Earthworm and cockroach are schizocoelous, and only the starfish adult is radial. (C) All four are true coelomates. (D) Echinoderms are triploblastic despite radial adult symmetry.
Key point: Schizocoelom → protostomes (annelids, arthropods); enterocoelom → deuterostomes (echinoderms, chordates); echinoderm larvae are bilateral.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The order of structures met when passing from outside to the nucleus in a mature plant cell and in an animal cell, and organelles present in only one of them
questions.question: Imagine a needle passing from outside into the nucleus of (i) a mature leaf mesophyll cell and (ii) a human liver cell. Which option gives the correct order of structures met and a correct comparison?
options: A) (i) plasma membrane → cell wall → nucleus; (ii) cell wall → plasma membrane → nucleus; both cells have centrioles and chloroplasts
B) (i) tonoplast → cell wall → plasma membrane → nucleus; (ii) plasma membrane → large central vacuole → nucleus
C) (i) cell wall → plasma membrane → cytoplasm with chloroplasts → nucleus; (ii) cell wall → plasma membrane → nucleus; both lack vacuoles

D) (i) cell wall (with middle lamella shared with neighbours) → plasma membrane → thin layer of cytoplasm with chloroplasts → nucleus, which often lies pushed to the side by a large central vacuole bounded by the tonoplast; (ii) plasma membrane → cytoplasm → nucleus, with no cell wall; the plant cell lacks centrioles, while the animal cell has centrioles but no plastids and only small vacuoles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Wall → membrane → peripheral cytoplasm → nucleus in the plant cell; membrane → cytoplasm → nucleus in the animal cell.
Concept: Plant cells possess a cell wall outside the plasma membrane, plastids and a large central vacuole, which are absent in animal cells. Animal cells have centrioles, which are absent in almost all plant cells. The middle lamella is a layer mainly of calcium pectate that holds neighbouring plant cells together. The vacuole is bound by a single membrane called the tonoplast and can occupy up to 90 per cent of the volume of a plant cell, pushing the cytoplasm and nucleus to the periphery.
Why: The wall is the outermost layer of a plant cell, so it is met first; the plasma membrane lies just inside it. Because the central vacuole takes up most of the space, the cytoplasm forms a thin layer and the nucleus is displaced to one side. An animal cell has no wall, so its plasma membrane is the outer boundary.
Why not the others: (A) The wall lies outside the plasma membrane, and animal cells have no wall or chloroplasts. (B) The tonoplast surrounds the vacuole inside the cell, and liver cells have no large central vacuole. (C) Animal cells have no wall, and plant cells have a prominent vacuole.
Key point: Plant cell: wall, plastids, large central vacuole, no centrioles; animal cell: no wall, centrioles present, small vacuoles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Using base pairing to find the composition of the complementary strand and of the whole duplex from the composition of one DNA strand, and recognising single-stranded genomes
questions.question: One strand of a DNA duplex has the composition A = 20 %, T = 30 %, G = 35 %, C = 15 %. A virus genome is found to contain A = 25 %, T = 33 %, G = 24 %, C = 18 %. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The complementary strand has A 20 %, T 30 %, G 35 %, C 15 %; the virus genome is double-stranded
B) The complementary strand has A 30 %, T 20 %, G 15 %, C 35 %; the whole duplex has A = T = 25 % and G = C = 25 %; the virus genome, with A ≠ T and G ≠ C, is single-stranded
C) The whole duplex has A 20 %, T 30 %, G 35 %, C 15 %, because both strands are identical
D) The complementary strand has A 35 %, T 15 %, G 20 %, C 30 %; the virus genome is double-stranded RNA
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Complementary strand A 30, T 20, G 15, C 35; duplex A = T = G = C = 25 %; the virus genome is single-stranded.
Given: Strand 1: A 20 %, T 30 %, G 35 %, C 15 %. Virus: A 25, T 33, G 24, C 18 (%).
Formula/Principle: In double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C (Chargaff's rule: A = T, G = C, and the purine total equals the pyrimidine total).
Step 1: Every A in strand 1 faces a T in strand 2, and so on: strand 2 has A = 30 % (opposite T), T = 20 %, G = 15 % (opposite C), C = 35 %.
Step 2: Whole duplex: A = (20 + 30)/2 = 25 %, T = (30 + 20)/2 = 25 %, G = (35 + 15)/2 = 25 %, C = (15 + 35)/2 = 25 %.
Step 3: Virus: A (25) ≠ T (33) and G (24) ≠ C (18); it contains T, so it is DNA, and the lack of Chargaff equality shows the strands are not paired: single-stranded DNA.
Concept: The two strands of DNA are complementary and antiparallel; the base sequence of one strand fixes the other. Chargaff's equalities hold for double-stranded DNA but not for the individual strands or for single-stranded genomes such as that of bacteriophage φX174.
Why: Base pairing makes the duplex composition the average of the two strands, so A = T and G = C in the duplex even when a single strand is very uneven.
Why not the others: (A) The complementary strand is not identical to the first. (C) The two strands are complementary, not identical. (D) The bases have been paired wrongly, and the presence of T rules out RNA.
Key point: Complementary strand: swap A↔T and G↔C; Chargaff's rule applies only to double-stranded nucleic acid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Feedback (allosteric) inhibition of the first enzyme of a pathway by its end product and the effect of a block at an intermediate enzyme
questions.question: In a bacterium, end product D is made by the pathway A → B → C → D, catalysed by enzymes E1, E2 and E3 respectively. D binds to E1 at a site other than its active site and switches it off. What happens in a mutant that lacks E2 when the cells are grown without D?
options: A) B accumulates and D is not made; E1 stays active

B) B accumulates and D is not made; since D is absent, E1 is not inhibited and keeps converting A to B, so B builds up; adding D to the medium switches E1 off and stops the build-up of B, while the cells can now grow using the supplied D
C) C accumulates; E1 is switched off by B
D) A accumulates, because E1 is competitively inhibited by B at its active site
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B accumulates; E1 remains active without D; added D switches E1 off and supports growth.
Concept: Enzymes are proteins with an active site where the substrate binds. When a molecule closely resembling the substrate binds the active site, it is a competitive inhibitor (for example malonate inhibiting succinic dehydrogenase). In feedback inhibition, the end product of a metabolic pathway binds the first enzyme of the pathway at a regulatory (allosteric) site, reducing its activity so that the product is not overproduced. Enzymes act in sequence in metabolic pathways, each product being the substrate of the next enzyme.
Why: Without E2, the pathway is blocked after B; the intermediate before the block piles up, and nothing beyond it is formed. Because the regulator D is never made, the first enzyme is never switched off. Supplying D both satisfies the cell's need and restores the feedback control.
Why not the others: (A) Incomplete: it misses what happens when D is supplied and why E1 stays active. (C) The block is before C, and B is not the regulator. (D) A is converted by an active E1; the inhibitor is D, acting allosterically.
Key point: A block in a pathway causes the substrate of the missing enzyme to accumulate; end-product feedback acts on the first enzyme.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the Emerson enhancement effect quantitatively as evidence for two photosystems working together in the light reaction
questions.question: In an experiment on an alga, the rate of O₂ evolution (arbitrary units) is 12 with red light of 680 nm alone, 4 with far-red light beyond 690 nm alone, and 24 when both beams are given together. What is the enhancement ratio and what does it show?
options: A) Ratio 0.5; the two wavelengths compete for the same pigment
B) Ratio 2.0; the two beams act on the same photosystem
C) Ratio 1.0; the effects are simply additive

D) Ratio 1.5 (24 ÷ 16); the combined rate is greater than the sum of the separate rates because two photosystems are involved — PS I, with reaction centre P700, absorbs the longer wavelength, and PS II, with reaction centre P680, the shorter — and they work in series in non-cyclic electron flow (the Z scheme) from water to NADP⁺
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Enhancement ratio = 24/(12 + 4) = 1.5; evidence for two photosystems in series.
Given: Rate (680 nm alone) = 12; rate (> 690 nm alone) = 4; rate (both together) = 24.
Formula/Principle: Enhancement ratio = rate with both beams ÷ (sum of rates with each beam alone).
Step 1: Sum of separate rates = 12 + 4 = 16.
Step 2: Enhancement ratio = 24/16 = 1.5.
Step 3: A ratio above 1 means the two beams help each other: each drives a different light reaction that the other needs.
Concept: The light reactions use two photosystems, PS I and PS II, named in the order of their discovery, not in the order in which they function. The reaction centre of PS I has chlorophyll a with an absorption peak at 700 nm (P700), and that of PS II has an absorption peak at 680 nm (P680). In non-cyclic photophosphorylation, electrons from PS II pass through an electron transport chain to PS I and then to NADP⁺; water splitting associated with PS II supplies electrons and releases O₂. The drop in O₂ evolution in light beyond 680 nm is the "red drop", and its recovery when shorter-wavelength light is added is the Emerson enhancement effect.
Why: Light beyond 690 nm excites mainly PS I, so electrons are drained from the chain but not replaced by PS II; combined with 680 nm light, both photosystems run and the chain from water to NADP⁺ works at full speed.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) Wrong arithmetic and interpretation. (B) The ratio is 1.5, and synergy indicates two different photosystems.
Key point: Enhancement ratio > 1 → two photosystems (P680 and P700) working in series.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The order of dedifferentiation, callus formation and redifferentiation in regenerating plants from explants, and the role of the auxin–cytokinin ratio
questions.question: A piece of mature leaf tissue (explant) is placed on a nutrient medium. Which sequence of events, and which hormonal control, is correct?
options: A) Mature non-dividing cells regain the capacity to divide (dedifferentiation) → they proliferate as an undifferentiated mass, the callus → callus cells again lose the capacity to divide and mature into specific cell types (redifferentiation), forming shoots and roots; a high cytokinin-to-auxin ratio favours shoots, and a high auxin-to-cytokinin ratio favours roots
B) Redifferentiation → callus → dedifferentiation; auxin alone always gives shoots
C) Callus → dedifferentiation → seed formation; cytokinin gives roots and auxin gives shoots
D) Explant cells divide only by meiosis, forming haploid shoots directly without a callus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Dedifferentiation → callus → redifferentiation; cytokinin favours shoots, auxin favours roots.
Concept: Cells derived from root apical and shoot apical meristems and cambium differentiate and mature to perform specific functions; this act leading to maturation is termed differentiation. Living differentiated cells that by now have lost the capacity to divide can regain the capacity of division under certain conditions; this phenomenon is termed dedifferentiation (for example, interfascicular cambium and cork cambium formed from fully differentiated parenchyma cells). Cells produced by such dedifferentiated tissue again lose the capacity to divide but mature to perform specific functions; this is redifferentiation. In tissue culture, the ratio of auxin to cytokinin decides the type of organ formed.
Why: Differentiation in plants is open: mature cells keep the genetic information to form a whole plant (totipotency), so with suitable hormones they first return to a dividing state and then form new organs.
Why not the others: (B) The order is reversed, and auxin alone favours roots. (C) The order is wrong, the hormones are swapped, and no seeds form. (D) Callus cells divide by mitosis.
Key point: Differentiation → dedifferentiation → callus → redifferentiation; cytokinin:auxin high → shoots, low → roots.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why alveolar ventilation, not total ventilation, measures useful breathing, using dead space to compare shallow rapid and deep slow breathing
questions.question: Two people each breathe 6000 mL of air per minute. P breathes 300 mL per breath at 20 breaths per minute; Q breathes 600 mL per breath at 10 breaths per minute. The anatomical dead space (air in trachea, bronchi and bronchioles not reaching the alveoli) is 150 mL in both. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Both ventilate their alveoli equally, since both move 6000 mL per minute
B) P has better alveolar ventilation because of its higher rate

C) Alveolar ventilation is 3000 mL/min for P and 4500 mL/min for Q, because the first 150 mL of each breath only refills the dead space and does not take part in gas exchange; deep slow breathing is therefore more effective
D) Alveolar ventilation is zero in P, because its tidal volume is less than the residual volume
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P: (300 − 150) × 20 = 3000 mL/min; Q: (600 − 150) × 10 = 4500 mL/min.
Given: Minute volume 6000 mL/min for both; P: TV 300 mL, rate 20; Q: TV 600 mL, rate 10; dead space 150 mL.
Formula/Principle: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × breathing rate.
Step 1: P: 300 − 150 = 150 mL of fresh air reaches the alveoli per breath; 150 × 20 = 3000 mL/min.
Step 2: Q: 600 − 150 = 450 mL per breath; 450 × 10 = 4500 mL/min.
Step 3: Same total ventilation, but Q delivers 50 % more fresh air to the alveoli.
Concept: Tidal volume is the volume of air inspired or expired during a normal respiration (about 500 mL in a healthy adult). The conducting part of the respiratory system (nose to terminal bronchioles) transports atmospheric air to the alveoli, clears it of foreign particles, humidifies it and brings it to body temperature, but no exchange of gases occurs there. The exchange part is the alveoli and their ducts. Residual volume is the air remaining in the lungs even after a forcible expiration.
Why: Each breath first pushes the stale air of the conducting zone into the alveoli; only the volume beyond the dead space is fresh. With small breaths a larger fraction of each breath is wasted.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores dead space. (B) Faster shallow breaths waste more air. (D) Tidal volume is compared with dead space, not residual volume.
Key point: Useful ventilation = (TV − dead space) × rate; deep breaths are more efficient.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why calcium chelators such as citrate prevent clotting of stored blood while added calcium restores it, and the role of thrombin and fibrin
questions.question: Blood collected in a blood bank bag containing sodium citrate (which binds Ca²⁺ ions) stays fluid for weeks. When CaCl₂ is added to a sample, it clots within minutes. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) Citrate destroys platelets, and Ca²⁺ ions are themselves converted into fibrin
B) Citrate converts fibrinogen into albumin, and Ca²⁺ dissolves the clot
C) Ca²⁺ ions are needed only for the contraction of the heart, not for clotting; the clot forms because citrate is diluted

D) The clotting cascade needs free Ca²⁺ ions: thrombokinase from damaged tissue and platelets, with Ca²⁺, converts inactive prothrombin into thrombin, and thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap blood cells; citrate removes free Ca²⁺ so thrombin cannot form, and adding excess Ca²⁺ restores the cascade
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Citrate binds the Ca²⁺ needed for prothrombin → thrombin; extra Ca²⁺ restarts the cascade.
Concept: Blood exhibits coagulation or clotting in response to an injury or trauma. A clot or coagulum is formed mainly of a network of threads called fibrins in which dead and damaged formed elements of blood are trapped. Fibrins are formed by the conversion of inactive fibrinogens in the plasma by the enzyme thrombin. Thrombins, in turn, are formed from another inactive substance present in the plasma called prothrombin. An enzyme complex, thrombokinase, is required for this reaction, and is formed by a series of linked enzymic reactions (a cascade process) involving a number of factors present in the plasma in an inactive state. An injury stimulates the platelets to release certain factors that activate the mechanism. Calcium ions play a very important role in clotting.
Why: Removing a necessary cofactor halts an enzyme cascade without damaging the proteins; restoring the cofactor lets the cascade proceed, which is why citrated blood can be used for transfusion.
Why not the others: (A) Citrate does not destroy platelets, and fibrin comes from fibrinogen. (B) Fibrinogen is not converted to albumin, and Ca²⁺ promotes clotting. (C) Ca²⁺ is a clotting factor; the clot forms because free Ca²⁺ is restored.
Key point: Ca²⁺ is essential for clotting: prothrombin → thrombin → fibrinogen → fibrin; citrate or oxalate prevents clotting by removing Ca²⁺.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table of animals, their main nitrogenous waste and their habitat to identify the correctly matched rows
questions.question:
Which rows of the table are correctly matched?
Row | Animal | Main nitrogenous waste | Reason
1 | Bony fish (freshwater) | Ammonia | Highly soluble, toxic waste easily lost by diffusion across gills into abundant water
2 | Mammal | Uric acid | Least toxic, excreted as a paste to save water
3 | Bird | Uric acid | Can be removed as a pellet or paste with minimal water loss; suits flight and shelled eggs
4 | Marine fish | Ammonia only, never urea | No need to conserve water in the sea
options: A) 1 and 4 only
B) 1 and 3 only
C) 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Rows 1 and 3.
Concept: Animals accumulate ammonia, urea, uric acid, carbon dioxide, water and ions as metabolic waste. Ammonia is the most toxic form and requires large amounts of water for its elimination, whereas uric acid, being the least toxic, can be removed with a minimum loss of water. The process of excreting ammonia is ammonotelism; many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects are ammonotelic. Ammonia, as it is readily soluble, is generally excreted by diffusion across body surfaces or through gill surfaces (in fish) as ammonium ions. Mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes mainly excrete urea and are called ureotelic animals. Reptiles, birds, land snails and insects excrete nitrogenous wastes as uric acid in the form of pellet or paste with a minimum loss of water and are called uricotelic animals.
Why: The form of nitrogenous waste depends on water availability: plentiful water allows toxic ammonia; water conservation favours urea or uric acid.
Why not the others: Row 2 is wrong because mammals are ureotelic. Row 4 is wrong because marine fishes are ureotelic. So (A), (C) and (D) all include a wrong row.
Key point: Ammonotelic: bony fish, aquatic amphibians; ureotelic: mammals, marine fish, terrestrial amphibians; uricotelic: birds, reptiles, insects.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table of hormones with the disorder caused by too little or too much of each
questions.question:
Which option gives all rows correctly?
Row | Hormone | Condition
1 | Growth hormone — excess in childhood | ?
2 | Thyroid hormone — deficiency during pregnancy/early childhood | ?
3 | Cortisol and aldosterone — deficiency | ?
4 | Insulin — deficiency | ?
options: A) 1 gigantism; 2 cretinism (stunted growth, mental retardation); 3 Addison's disease; 4 diabetes mellitus with hyperglycaemia
B) 1 dwarfism; 2 exophthalmic goitre; 3 Cushing's syndrome; 4 hypoglycaemia
C) 1 acromegaly; 2 Graves' disease; 3 diabetes insipidus; 4 tetany
D) 1 gigantism; 2 Graves' disease; 3 Addison's disease; 4 diabetes insipidus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Gigantism; cretinism; Addison's disease; diabetes mellitus.
Concept: Excess secretion of growth hormone stimulates abnormal growth of the body leading to gigantism, and low secretion of GH results in stunted growth resulting in pituitary dwarfism. Excess GH in adults, especially in middle age, can result in severe disfigurement (acromegaly). Hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development and maturation of the growing baby, leading to stunted growth (cretinism), mental retardation, low intelligence quotient and abnormal skin. Hyperthyroidism can result from cancer of the thyroid or nodules; exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism. Underproduction of hormones by the adrenal cortex alters carbohydrate metabolism, causing acute weakness and fatigue, leading to Addison's disease. Prolonged hyperglycaemia leads to a complex disorder called diabetes mellitus. Diabetes insipidus results from impaired ADH secretion.
Why: Each disorder follows from what the hormone normally does: GH drives growth, thyroid hormones drive development and metabolism, corticoids maintain metabolism and salt balance, and insulin lowers blood glucose.
Why not the others: (B) Excess GH causes gigantism, not dwarfism; low thyroid causes cretinism; insulin deficiency causes hyperglycaemia. (C) Acromegaly is adult excess; Graves' disease is hyperthyroidism; diabetes insipidus is due to ADH. (D) Graves' disease is hyperthyroidism, and diabetes insipidus is not due to insulin.
Key point: Childhood GH excess → gigantism; foetal/infant hypothyroidism → cretinism; adrenal cortex deficiency → Addison's; insulin deficiency → diabetes mellitus.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing nucellar polyembryony in citrus, apomixis and parthenocarpy in seedless fruits, and the genetic make-up of the resulting seedlings
questions.question: A citrus seed produces four seedlings: one from the fertilised egg and three from nucellus cells. A banana variety forms fruits without seeds. Which comparison is correct?
options: A) All four citrus seedlings are genetically identical to the pollen parent; banana fruits develop after double fertilisation
B) The citrus seedlings are all haploid; banana fruits contain small viable seeds

C) The three nucellar seedlings are genetically identical to the mother plant (clones, formed by apomixis without fertilisation), whereas the zygotic seedling carries genes of both parents; the occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed is polyembryony; the seedless banana is parthenocarpic — the fruit develops without fertilisation and without seed formation
D) Polyembryony and parthenocarpy are the same process, since both avoid fertilisation and both give seeds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Nucellar embryos are maternal clones; the zygotic embryo is recombinant; banana is parthenocarpic.
Concept: Although seeds in general are the products of fertilisation, a few flowering plants such as some species of Asteraceae and grasses have evolved a special mechanism to produce seeds without fertilisation, called apomixis; thus apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction. In many species, such as citrus and mango varieties, some of the nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos; in such species each ovule contains many embryos. The occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed is referred to as polyembryony. A few species such as banana produce fruits without fertilisation; such fruits are parthenocarpic fruits. Parthenocarpy can be induced through the application of growth hormones, and such fruits are seedless.
Why: Nucellus is maternal diploid tissue, so embryos from it carry exactly the mother's genotype; the zygote combines egg and sperm. A parthenocarpic fruit develops from the ovary wall without fertilised ovules, so no seeds form.
Why not the others: (A) Nucellar seedlings match the mother, not the pollen parent, and parthenocarpic fruits form without fertilisation. (B) Nucellar and zygotic embryos are diploid, and seedless bananas have no viable seeds. (D) Polyembryony gives extra embryos in seeds; parthenocarpy gives fruits without seeds.
Key point: Nucellar embryo = maternal clone (apomixis); polyembryony = many embryos in one seed; parthenocarpy = seedless fruit without fertilisation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Mechanisms of spermatogenesis: the scrotal temperature, the roles of LH on Leydig cells and FSH on Sertoli cells, and meiotic output from one primary spermatocyte
questions.question: A man with undescended testes (remaining in the abdominal cavity) produces no sperm, although his testosterone level is nearly normal. Which explanation, and which accompanying statement about spermatogenesis, is correct?
options: A) Spermatogenesis needs a temperature about 2–2.5 °C below body temperature, which the scrotum provides; Leydig cells, stimulated by LH, can still secrete androgens at body temperature, which explains the near-normal testosterone; normally FSH acts on Sertoli cells, which nourish the developing germ cells, and each primary spermatocyte gives four spermatids after meiosis, which become sperms by spermiogenesis
B) Leydig cells form sperms directly; LH acts on Sertoli cells; one primary spermatocyte gives one sperm
C) Spermatogenesis needs a temperature higher than body temperature; testosterone is made by Sertoli cells
D) Sperm are produced only in the epididymis; FSH inhibits spermatogenesis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Too high a temperature blocks spermatogenesis, while Leydig cells still make androgens; one primary spermatocyte → four spermatids → four sperms.
Concept: The testes are situated outside the abdominal cavity within a pouch called the scrotum, which helps in maintaining the low temperature of the testes (2–2.5 °C lower than the normal internal body temperature) necessary for spermatogenesis. Each seminiferous tubule is lined on its inside by male germ cells (spermatogonia) and Sertoli cells, which provide nutrition to the germ cells. The regions outside the seminiferous tubules contain interstitial or Leydig cells, which synthesise and secrete testicular hormones called androgens. At puberty, increased GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH; LH acts on the Leydig cells and stimulates synthesis and secretion of androgens, and FSH acts on the Sertoli cells and stimulates secretion of some factors which help in the process of spermiogenesis. A primary spermatocyte completes the first meiotic division (reduction division) leading to two equal haploid secondary spermatocytes, which undergo the second meiotic division to produce four equal haploid spermatids. The spermatids are transformed into spermatozoa (sperms) by spermiogenesis.
Why: Germ-cell meiosis is temperature-sensitive, but hormone synthesis by Leydig cells is not, so an abdominal testis keeps endocrine function while losing sperm production.
Why not the others: (B) Leydig cells make androgens, LH acts on Leydig cells, and one primary spermatocyte gives four sperms. (C) The required temperature is lower, and testosterone comes from Leydig cells. (D) Sperms are produced in seminiferous tubules (they mature in the epididymis), and FSH supports spermatogenesis.
Key point: Scrotum keeps testes 2–2.5 °C cooler; LH → Leydig → androgens; FSH → Sertoli → spermiogenesis; 1 primary spermatocyte → 4 sperms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Proportions of normal and aneuploid gametes produced by non-disjunction in meiosis I versus meiosis II, and the chromosome numbers of the resulting zygotes
questions.question: In a human oocyte-forming cell, the chromosome 21 pair fails to separate. Considering all four products of meiosis, what fraction of gametes is abnormal if the failure is in meiosis I, and if it is in meiosis II (in one of the two secondary cells)? If an n + 1 gamete with an extra chromosome 21 is fertilised by a normal sperm, what is the chromosome number of the zygote?
options: A) Meiosis I: half abnormal; meiosis II: all abnormal; zygote 45
B) Meiosis I: none abnormal; meiosis II: half abnormal; zygote 46
C) Meiosis I: one quarter abnormal; meiosis II: one quarter abnormal; zygote 48
D) Meiosis I: all four abnormal (two n + 1 and two n − 1); meiosis II: half abnormal (one n + 1, one n − 1 and two normal n); zygote 47 with trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Meiosis I non-disjunction: 4/4 abnormal; meiosis II: 2/4 abnormal; zygote 2n + 1 = 47 (Down's syndrome).
Given: Normal human gamete n = 23; non-disjunction of chromosome 21.
Formula/Principle: Meiosis I separates homologues; meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Non-disjunction gives gametes with n + 1 and n − 1 chromosomes.
Step 1: Meiosis I failure: both homologues go to one secondary cell (n + 1) and none to the other (n − 1); each then divides normally → two n + 1 and two n − 1 gametes: all four abnormal.
Step 2: Meiosis II failure in one secondary cell: that cell gives one n + 1 and one n − 1; the other secondary cell divides normally → two n. So 2 of 4 abnormal.
Step 3: n + 1 egg (24) + normal sperm (23) = 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21.
Concept: Failure of segregation of chromatids during the cell division cycle results in the gain or loss of a chromosome(s), called aneuploidy. Down's syndrome is caused by the presence of an additional copy of chromosome number 21 (trisomy of 21); affected individuals are short statured with a small round head, furrowed tongue and partially open mouth, and physical, psychomotor and mental development is retarded. Turner's syndrome (45, X0) and Klinefelter's syndrome (47, XXY) arise similarly from non-disjunction of sex chromosomes.
Why: The earlier the error, the more products inherit it: a meiosis I error affects both daughter lines, a meiosis II error only one.
Why not the others: (A) Fractions reversed and wrong zygote number. (B) A meiosis I error makes all gametes abnormal. (C) Wrong fractions; 48 would need two extra chromosomes.
Key point: Non-disjunction in meiosis I → all 4 gametes aneuploid; in meiosis II → 2 of 4; n + 1 gamete × n → 2n + 1.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the number of repeats in VNTR alleles from fragment sizes and the probability of a chance match across several independent loci in DNA fingerprinting
questions.question: At one VNTR locus the repeat unit is 16 bp and the flanking DNA included in each fragment is 100 bp. A suspect's fragments are 420 bp and 580 bp. Across three independent loci the suspect's genotype frequencies in the population are 0.01, 0.05 and 0.02. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The alleles carry 26 and 36 repeats; the chance-match probability is 0.08, since the frequencies add
B) The alleles carry 20 and 30 repeats; the chance-match probability is 1 × 10⁻³

C) The alleles carry 20 and 30 repeats; the chance-match probability is 0.01 × 0.05 × 0.02 = 1 × 10⁻⁵, so in a city of 2 million people about 20 unrelated individuals would be expected to match by chance — which is why many more loci are used in practice
D) The alleles carry 26 and 36 repeats; a match at three loci proves identity with certainty
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 20 and 30 repeats; match probability 1 × 10⁻⁵; about 20 chance matches in 2 million.
Given: Repeat = 16 bp; flanking = 100 bp; fragments 420 and 580 bp; genotype frequencies 0.01, 0.05, 0.02.
Formula/Principle: Number of repeats = (fragment − flanking)/repeat length. For independent loci, probabilities multiply (product rule).
Step 1: (420 − 100)/16 = 320/16 = 20 repeats; (580 − 100)/16 = 480/16 = 30 repeats.
Step 2: P(chance match) = 0.01 × 0.05 × 0.02 = 1 × 10⁻⁵.
Step 3: Expected chance matches in 2 × 10⁶ people = 2 × 10⁶ × 10⁻⁵ = 20.
Concept: DNA fingerprinting involves identifying differences in some specific regions of the DNA sequence called repetitive DNA, because in these sequences a small stretch of DNA is repeated many times. Satellite DNA is classified on the basis of base composition, length of segment and number of repetitive units into categories such as micro-satellites and mini-satellites. These sequences show a high degree of polymorphism, and VNTR (variable number of tandem repeats) belongs to the mini-satellite class; the copy number varies from chromosome to chromosome in an individual, so the size of a VNTR varies. After hybridisation with a VNTR probe, bands of different sizes give the characteristic pattern of an individual DNA.
Why: Each additional locus multiplies the rarity of the combined profile, so a few loci can leave several chance matches in a large population, while many loci make chance matches negligible.
Why not the others: (A) Forgets to subtract the flanking DNA, and independent probabilities multiply, not add. (B) The product is 10⁻⁵, not 10⁻³. (D) Wrong repeat numbers; a three-locus match is strong but not certain evidence.
Key point: Repeats = (size − flank)/unit; match probability = product of genotype frequencies at independent loci.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The logical sequence of the RNA world hypothesis — from catalytic RNA to DNA as the stable genetic material — and the Central Dogma with its exception
questions.question: Which sequence and reasoning about the evolution of genetic material is correct?
options: A) DNA arose first as a catalyst; RNA evolved later because it is more stable; information flows only from protein to DNA

B) RNA was the first genetic material and could also act as a catalyst (as ribozymes still do); because RNA is reactive and unstable (its 2′-OH group) and mutates fast, DNA evolved from RNA with chemical changes — deoxyribose and thymine in place of uracil — that make it more stable, and proteins took over most catalysis; the Central Dogma states DNA → RNA → protein, with reverse transcription (RNA → DNA) in retroviruses as an exception
C) Proteins were the first genetic material; DNA evolved because proteins cannot fold
D) RNA and DNA arose at the same time; uracil was replaced by thymine because thymine is more reactive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) RNA first (genetic + catalytic) → DNA for stability (deoxyribose, thymine) → proteins as main catalysts; DNA → RNA → protein, with reverse transcription as an exception.
Concept: RNA was the first genetic material. There is now enough evidence to suggest that essential life processes such as metabolism, translation and splicing evolved around RNA. RNA used to act as a genetic material as well as a catalyst; there are some important biochemical reactions in living systems that are catalysed by RNA catalysts and not by protein enzymes. But RNA being a catalyst was reactive and hence unstable. Therefore DNA has evolved from RNA with chemical modifications that make it more stable. Presence of thymine at the place of uracil also confers additional stability to DNA. The 2′-OH group present at every nucleotide in RNA is a reactive group and makes RNA labile and easily degradable. Francis Crick proposed the Central Dogma: genetic information flows from DNA → RNA → protein. In some viruses the flow of information is in the reverse direction, that is, from RNA to DNA.
Why: Stability is essential for long-term storage of information, while reactivity is useful for catalysis; DNA and proteins each specialise in one of the two roles RNA once combined.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the stability argument and the direction of information flow. (C) Proteins cannot replicate themselves as templates. (D) Thymine makes DNA more stable, not more reactive, and RNA came first.
Key point: RNA world → DNA (stable: deoxyribose, thymine) and proteins (catalysis); Central Dogma DNA → RNA → protein; retroviruses reverse-transcribe.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting an observed change in allele frequency on an island as gene flow (migration) and predicting genotype frequencies after random mating
questions.question: An island population has allele frequency q(a) = 0.20. Migrants from the mainland, where q = 0.60, arrive and come to make up 25 % of the island population, after which mating is random. What is the new q, and what are the expected genotype frequencies in the next generation?
options: A) q stays 0.20, because migration does not change allele frequencies; aa = 0.04

B) q = 0.30, because 0.75 × 0.20 + 0.25 × 0.60 = 0.30; after one generation of random mating AA = 0.49, Aa = 0.42, aa = 0.09; the change is due to gene flow, one of the factors that disturb Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
C) q = 0.40, the simple average of 0.20 and 0.60; aa = 0.16
D) q = 0.60, because migrants replace the residents; aa = 0.36
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) q = 0.30; AA 0.49, Aa 0.42, aa 0.09; gene flow.
Given: Residents: q = 0.20, fraction 0.75; migrants: q = 0.60, fraction 0.25.
Formula/Principle: Mixed q = weighted average of the allele frequencies; Hardy–Weinberg after random mating: p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
Step 1: q = 0.75 × 0.20 + 0.25 × 0.60 = 0.15 + 0.15 = 0.30.
Step 2: p = 1 − 0.30 = 0.70.
Step 3: AA = 0.70² = 0.49; Aa = 2 × 0.70 × 0.30 = 0.42; aa = 0.30² = 0.09.
Concept: Hardy–Weinberg principle says that allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation; the gene pool remains constant, which is called genetic equilibrium. Five factors are known to affect Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection. When migration of a section of population to another place and population occurs, gene frequencies change in the original as well as in the new population; new genes or alleles are added to the new population and lost from the old population. There would be a gene flow if this gene migration happens multiple times.
Why: Allele frequency is a property of the whole gene pool, so mixing two pools gives a frequency weighted by their sizes; one round of random mating then restores Hardy–Weinberg genotype proportions at the new frequency.
Why not the others: (A) Migration does change allele frequencies. (C) The average must be weighted by the 75 : 25 proportion. (D) The migrants are only a quarter of the population.
Key point: Gene flow: new q = weighted average; random mating then gives p², 2pq, q².

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting an experiment showing primary and secondary antibody responses, the specificity of memory, and the difference from allergy
questions.question: Mice are injected with antigen X on day 0. On day 30 they are injected again with X and, for the first time, with an unrelated antigen Y. Antibody levels are measured. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The responses to X and Y on day 30 are identical, because both are injections
B) The response to Y is faster than to X on day 30, because Y is new

C) After day 30, anti-X antibody rises faster and to a much higher level than after day 0 (secondary, anamnestic response from memory B and T cells), while anti-Y shows a slow, low primary response, because memory is specific to the antigen first met; this is the basis of vaccination, and it differs from an allergy, in which IgE antibodies bound to mast cells release histamine and serotonin on exposure to an allergen
D) Both responses on day 30 are primary, since the immune system has no memory
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Secondary response to X, primary response to Y; memory is antigen-specific.
Concept: When our body encounters a pathogen for the first time it produces a response called primary response, which is of low intensity. Subsequent encounter with the same pathogen elicits a highly intensified secondary or anamnestic response. This is ascribed to the fact that our body appears to have memory of the first encounter. The principle of immunisation or vaccination is based on the property of memory of the immune system. The exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens present in the environment is called allergy; the substances to which such an immune response is produced are called allergens. The antibodies produced to these are of IgE type. Allergy is due to the release of chemicals like histamine and serotonin from the mast cells.
Why: Memory cells formed after the first exposure to X recognise only X; Y is met for the first time, so it must start from naïve lymphocytes.
Why not the others: (A) Memory makes the X response stronger. (B) A new antigen gives the slower primary response. (D) The adaptive immune system has memory.
Key point: Secondary response is faster, stronger and antigen-specific; allergy involves IgE, mast cells and histamine.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The order of steps from culturing recombinant cells in a bioreactor to obtaining a marketable protein, and the purpose of each part of a stirred-tank reactor
questions.question: A recombinant protein is to be produced and sold. Which sequence and description are correct?
options: A) Formulation → separation → culture → purification; a stirred-tank reactor has a flat base to stop mixing
B) Purification → culture → clinical trials → separation; sparged reactors bubble nitrogen to remove oxygen
C) Culture in small flasks only; downstream processing is not needed because the product is already pure

D) Large-scale culture in a bioreactor (for example a stirred-tank reactor — usually cylindrical or with a curved base to help mixing, with an agitator, an oxygen delivery (sparging) system and controls for temperature, pH, foam and sampling) → separation of product → purification → formulation with suitable preservatives → strict quality control and clinical trials (for drugs) before marketing
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Culture → separation → purification → formulation → quality control/clinical trials.
Concept: Small volumes of cultures cannot yield appreciable quantities of products; to produce in large quantities, bioreactors, where large volumes (100–1000 litres) of culture can be processed, are needed. A bioreactor provides the optimal conditions for achieving the desired product by providing optimum growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen). The most commonly used bioreactors are of stirring type. A stirred-tank reactor is usually cylindrical or with a curved base to facilitate the mixing of the reactor contents; the stirrer facilitates even mixing and oxygen availability throughout the bioreactor. Alternatively, air can be bubbled through the reactor. The bioreactor has an agitator system, an oxygen delivery system and a foam control system, a temperature control system, a pH control system and sampling ports. After completion of the biosynthetic stage, the product has to be subjected through a series of processes before it is ready for marketing; the processes include separation and purification, which are collectively referred to as downstream processing. The product has to be formulated with suitable preservatives. Such formulation has to undergo thorough clinical trials as in the case of drugs. Strict quality control testing for each product is also required.
Why: A product must first be made in quantity, then recovered from the broth, cleaned of contaminants, stabilised for storage, and proven safe before sale.
Why not the others: (A) Order wrong; a curved base aids mixing. (B) Order wrong; sparging supplies air/oxygen. (C) Flask cultures give too little, and the broth must be processed downstream.
Key point: Upstream (culture in bioreactor) → downstream (separation, purification) → formulation → QC and trials.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of events by which competition between two species leads to resource partitioning or character displacement instead of exclusion
questions.question: Two species of seed-eating birds with similar beak sizes come to live on the same island and compete for seeds. Which sequence of events, leading to their coexistence, is most consistent with competition theory?
options: A) Overlap in diet causes competition → individuals of each species that use the seeds less used by the other species leave more offspring → over generations the beak sizes of the two species diverge (character displacement) and they partition the resource → reduced competition allows coexistence; without such divergence, Gause's competitive exclusion principle predicts that the inferior competitor would eventually be eliminated
B) Competition causes both species to converge in beak size → they then coexist using identical seeds
C) One species immediately becomes a predator of the other → coexistence follows
D) Competition has no effect because each bird eats only a few seeds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Competition → selection for divergent beaks → resource partitioning → coexistence; otherwise exclusion.
Concept: Competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured in terms of its 'r', the intrinsic rate of increase) is significantly lower in the presence of another species. Gause's 'Competitive Exclusion Principle' states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually. More recent studies show that species facing competition might evolve mechanisms that promote co-existence rather than exclusion; one such mechanism is resource partitioning. If two species compete for the same resource, they could avoid competition by choosing, for instance, different times for feeding or different foraging patterns. MacArthur showed that five closely related species of warblers living on the same tree were able to avoid competition and co-exist due to behavioural differences in their foraging activities.
Why: Selection favours individuals that compete least, so the two species shift apart in the trait that determines resource use; this lowers niche overlap enough for both to persist.
Why not the others: (B) Convergence would increase competition. (C) Competition does not turn into predation. (D) Shared limiting resources make competition significant.
Key point: Competition → exclusion, or → divergence/resource partitioning → coexistence.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Zero-order surface decomposition of ammonia followed by pressure: half-life, total pressure at a given time, time for completion and dependence of half-life on initial pressure
questions.question: Ammonia decomposes on a hot tungsten surface, 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g), by zero-order kinetics. Starting with pure NH₃ at 0.40 atm, its pressure falls at a constant 1.0 × 10⁻³ atm s⁻¹. Which statement is correct?
options: A) t½ = 200 s; at 100 s the total pressure is 0.50 atm; the NH₃ is used up at 400 s; with 0.80 atm initially, t½ would be 400 s
B) t½ = 693 s; at 100 s the total pressure is 0.40 atm; the reaction never finishes
C) t½ = 200 s; at 100 s the total pressure is 0.30 atm; with 0.80 atm initially, t½ would still be 200 s
D) t½ = 400 s; at 100 s the total pressure is 0.60 atm; the NH₃ is used up at 800 s
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) t½ = 200 s; P_total(100 s) = 0.50 atm; complete at 400 s; t½ doubles to 400 s for 0.80 atm.
Concept: In a zero-order reaction the rate is independent of the concentration of the reactant, and the concentration (or partial pressure) falls linearly with time: [R] = [R]₀ − kt. The half-life is t½ = [R]₀/2k, proportional to the initial concentration. The decomposition of gaseous ammonia on a hot platinum or tungsten surface at high pressure is a zero-order reaction because the metal surface becomes saturated with gas molecules, so the rate is fixed by the available surface.
Given: p₀(NH₃) = 0.40 atm; k = 1.0 × 10⁻³ atm s⁻¹ (rate of fall of p(NH₃)).
Formula/Principle: p(NH₃) = p₀ − kt; t½ = p₀/2k; stoichiometry 2NH₃ → N₂ + 3H₂.
Step 1: t½ = 0.40/(2 × 1.0 × 10⁻³) = 200 s.
Step 2: At 100 s, p(NH₃) = 0.40 − 0.10 = 0.30 atm; NH₃ used = 0.10 atm, giving N₂ = 0.05 atm and H₂ = 0.15 atm; total = 0.30 + 0.05 + 0.15 = 0.50 atm.
Step 3: Completion: p(NH₃) = 0 when t = 0.40/1.0 × 10⁻³ = 400 s; with p₀ = 0.80 atm, t½ = 0.80/(2 × 10⁻³) = 400 s.
Why: A saturated surface reacts at a fixed rate, so equal amounts disappear in equal times; for every 2 mol NH₃ lost, 4 mol gas form, so total pressure rises.
Why not the others: (B) Uses the first-order relation; a zero-order reaction goes to completion in a finite time. (C) Ignores the gaseous products, and t½ depends on p₀ in zero order. (D) Half-life and completion time are doubled.
Key point: Zero order: linear fall, t½ = [R]₀/2k ∝ [R]₀, completion at [R]₀/k.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining colour and magnetic behaviour of transition metal ions from d-electron count, ligands and charge transfer, and ordering paramagnetism by unpaired electrons
questions.question: Which set of observations and explanations is entirely correct?
options: A) Zn²⁺ salts are blue because Zn²⁺ has five unpaired electrons; Mn²⁺ is diamagnetic
B) KMnO₄ is colourless, since Mn(VII) has no d electrons; Sc³⁺ compounds are deeply coloured
C) Anhydrous CuSO₄ is blue and the hydrated salt is white; Cu²⁺ has three unpaired electrons

D) Hydrated CuSO₄ is blue (d⁹ Cu²⁺ with water ligands allows d–d transitions in the visible region) while anhydrous CuSO₄ is white; Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰) and Sc³⁺ (3d⁰) are colourless and diamagnetic; MnO₄⁻ is intensely purple despite 3d⁰ because of charge transfer from oxygen to manganese; paramagnetism decreases in the order Mn²⁺ (5 unpaired) > Fe²⁺ (4) > Cr³⁺ (3) > Cu²⁺ (1)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) d–d transitions need a partly filled d subshell and ligands; d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions are colourless; MnO₄⁻ colour is charge transfer; paramagnetism follows unpaired electrons.
Concept: When an electron from a lower energy d orbital is excited to a higher energy d orbital, the energy of excitation corresponds to the frequency of light absorbed, which generally lies in the visible region; the colour observed corresponds to the complementary colour of the light absorbed. The frequency of the light absorbed is determined by the nature of the ligand. In aqueous solutions, water molecules are the ligands. Paramagnetism arises from the presence of unpaired electrons, each such electron having a magnetic moment associated with its spin angular momentum and orbital angular momentum; the spin-only magnetic moment is μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
Given: Configurations: Mn²⁺ 3d⁵, Fe²⁺ 3d⁶, Cr³⁺ 3d³, Cu²⁺ 3d⁹, Zn²⁺ 3d¹⁰, Sc³⁺ 3d⁰, Mn(VII) 3d⁰.
Why: Without ligands around Cu²⁺ (anhydrous salt) the splitting of d levels changes so that absorption is no longer in the visible region; with no d electrons or a full d subshell, no d–d transition is possible. In MnO₄⁻, an electron moves from a ligand (O) orbital to the metal, a strongly allowed process that gives intense colour.
Why not the others: (A) Zn²⁺ has no unpaired electrons and is colourless; Mn²⁺ has five unpaired electrons. (B) KMnO₄ is intensely coloured; Sc³⁺ is colourless. (C) Hydrated CuSO₄ is blue and Cu²⁺ has one unpaired electron.
Key point: Colour: d–d (needs dⁿ, 0 < n < 10, with ligands) or charge transfer; paramagnetism ∝ number of unpaired electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Werner's primary and secondary valences, oxidation state and coordination number of given complexes, and ambidentate and polydentate ligands
questions.question: The complexes [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺, [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ and [Ni(CO)₄] and the ligands NO₂⁻, SCN⁻ and EDTA⁴⁻ are considered in terms of Werner's theory. Which statement is correct?
options: A) In [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ the coordination number of cobalt is 4 and its oxidation state is +1; SCN⁻ is a hexadentate ligand

B) Werner's primary valence (ionisable) corresponds to the oxidation state and the secondary valence (non-ionisable, directed in space) to the coordination number; in [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ cobalt is +3 with coordination number 6 (each en is bidentate); in [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ iron is +3 with coordination number 6; NO₂⁻ and SCN⁻ are ambidentate ligands, and EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate; in [Ni(CO)₄] nickel is 0 with coordination number 4
C) Primary valence equals the coordination number; in [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ iron is +6 with coordination number 3
D) Secondary valences are satisfied only by negative ions; CO cannot be a ligand because it is neutral
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Primary valence = oxidation state; secondary = coordination number; Co(III) CN 6; Fe(III) CN 6; NO₂⁻, SCN⁻ ambidentate; EDTA hexadentate; Ni(0) CN 4.
Concept: Werner proposed that in coordination compounds metals show two types of linkages (valences): primary and secondary. The primary valences are normally ionisable and are satisfied by negative ions. The secondary valences are non-ionisable; they are satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions, and the secondary valence is equal to the coordination number and is fixed for a metal. The ions or groups bound by the secondary linkages have characteristic spatial arrangements corresponding to different coordination numbers. When a ligand is bound through two donor atoms, as in H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂ (ethane-1,2-diamine) or C₂O₄²⁻ (oxalate), it is didentate; ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion (EDTA⁴⁻) is an important hexadentate ligand. A ligand which can ligate through two different atoms is called an ambidentate ligand; examples are NO₂⁻ and SCN⁻.
Given: en and C₂O₄²⁻ are bidentate; Cl⁻ and C₂O₄²⁻ carry −1 and −2; en and CO are neutral.
Step 1: [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺: x + 0 + 2(−1) = +1 ⇒ x = +3; donor atoms = 2 × 2 + 2 = 6.
Step 2: [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻: x + 3(−2) = −3 ⇒ x = +3; donor atoms = 3 × 2 = 6.
Step 3: [Ni(CO)₄]: x + 0 = 0 ⇒ x = 0; four CO ⇒ coordination number 4.
Why: The coordination number counts donor atoms, not ligands, so a bidentate ligand contributes two; the oxidation state comes from the charge balance of the complex ion.
Why not the others: (A) Each en contributes two donor atoms; SCN⁻ is monodentate (ambidentate). (C) The primary valence is the oxidation state, and the oxidation state and coordination number are miscounted. (D) Secondary valences can be satisfied by neutral ligands such as NH₃ or CO.
Key point: CN = number of donor atoms; oxidation state from charge balance; ambidentate: NO₂⁻, SCN⁻; EDTA⁴⁻ hexadentate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linking the acidity order of substituted phenols to their reactions with NaOH and NaHCO₃
questions.question: Phenol (pKa 10.0), p-nitrophenol (pKa 7.1), p-cresol (pKa 10.2), picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol, pKa 0.4) and ethanol (pKa about 16) are compared, with carbonic acid having pKa 6.4. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Ethanol is the strongest acid; phenol dissolves in aqueous NaHCO₃ with effervescence
B) p-Cresol is more acidic than phenol, because the methyl group withdraws electrons; picric acid does not react with NaHCO₃

C) Acidity order: picric acid > p-nitrophenol > phenol > p-cresol > ethanol; phenol dissolves in aqueous NaOH but not in NaHCO₃ (it is weaker than carbonic acid), whereas picric acid, being far stronger than carbonic acid, dissolves in NaHCO₃ with evolution of CO₂
D) All phenols are equally acidic because they all have an —OH group on a benzene ring
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Picric acid > p-nitrophenol > phenol > p-cresol > ethanol; phenol reacts with NaOH only, picric acid also with NaHCO₃.
Concept: The reactions of phenol with metals (sodium, aluminium) and sodium hydroxide indicate its acidic nature. The hydroxyl group in phenol is directly attached to the sp² hybridised carbon of the benzene ring, which acts as an electron-withdrawing group, and the phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge. The presence of electron-withdrawing groups such as the nitro group enhances the acidic strength of phenol; this effect is more pronounced when such a group is present at ortho and para positions, owing to effective delocalisation of the negative charge in the phenoxide ion. Electron-releasing groups, such as alkyl groups, in general do not favour the formation of the phenoxide ion, resulting in a decrease in acid strength. The greater the pKa value, the weaker the acid.
Given: pKa in increasing order: picric acid 0.4 < carbonic acid 6.4 < p-nitrophenol 7.1 < phenol 10.0 < p-cresol 10.2 < ethanol ≈ 16.
Step 1: Lower pKa = stronger acid, which gives the order in (C).
Step 2: An acid displaces CO₂ from HCO₃⁻ only if it is stronger than carbonic acid (pKa < 6.4): picric acid does, phenol does not.
Step 3: All phenols (pKa < 15.7 of water) react with NaOH to form phenoxide.
Why: Nitro groups withdraw electron density and delocalise the negative charge of the phenoxide ion, stabilising it; methyl groups push electrons in and destabilise it; the ethoxide ion has no resonance stabilisation.
Why not the others: (A) Ethanol is the weakest, and phenol does not react with NaHCO₃. (B) The methyl group is electron-releasing, and picric acid does react with NaHCO₃. (D) Substituents change acidity widely.
Key point: Electron-withdrawing groups (o/p-NO₂) increase phenol acidity; only acids stronger than H₂CO₃ liberate CO₂ from NaHCO₃.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Bromination and nitration of phenol under different conditions, the activating and ortho/para-directing role of –OH, and separation of o- and p-nitrophenol
questions.question: Which statement about electrophilic substitution in phenol is correct, with the right reason?
options: A) Phenol does not react with bromine water, because –OH deactivates the ring; dilute HNO₃ gives only m-nitrophenol
B) Phenol gives only m-bromophenol with Br₂ in CS₂, because –OH is meta-directing

C) With bromine water phenol gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, but with Br₂ in CS₂ at low temperature it gives mainly o- and p-bromophenol; with dilute HNO₃ it gives o- and p-nitrophenol, which are separated by steam distillation because o-nitrophenol is steam volatile owing to intramolecular hydrogen bonding; the –OH group activates the ring and directs to ortho and para positions by its +R effect
D) Concentrated HNO₃ converts phenol into benzoic acid, and o- and p-nitrophenol cannot be separated
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Bromine water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol; Br₂/CS₂ → mono-bromophenols; dilute HNO₃ → o- and p-nitrophenol, separated by steam distillation.
Concept: The –OH group attached to the benzene ring activates it towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions in the ring, as these positions become electron rich due to the resonance effect caused by the –OH group. With dilute nitric acid at low temperature (298 K), phenol yields a mixture of ortho and para nitrophenols. The ortho and para isomers can be separated by steam distillation: o-nitrophenol is steam volatile due to intramolecular hydrogen bonding, while p-nitrophenol is less volatile due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding, which causes association of molecules. With concentrated nitric acid, phenol is converted to 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid). When the reaction of phenol with bromine is carried out in solvents of low polarity such as CHCl₃ or CS₂ at low temperature, monobromophenols are formed; when phenol is treated with bromine water, 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed as a white precipitate.
Why: In water phenol partly ionises to phenoxide, which is even more strongly activating, and the polar solvent helps polarise Br₂, so all three o/p positions are substituted; in a non-polar solvent at low temperature the reaction can be stopped at monosubstitution.
Why not the others: (A) –OH is strongly activating and o/p-directing. (B) Products are o and p, not meta. (D) Concentrated HNO₃ gives picric acid, and the isomers are separable by steam distillation.
Key point: –OH: activating, o/p-directing; bromine water → tribromophenol; Br₂/CS₂ → mono; o-nitrophenol is steam volatile (intramolecular H-bond).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reduction of aldehydes and ketones to primary and secondary alcohols, why aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent, and vigorous oxidation of ketones with C–C cleavage
questions.question: Which set of statements about butanal and butanone is correct, with the right reasons?
options: A) NaBH₄ reduces butanal to butan-1-ol (a primary alcohol) and butanone to butan-2-ol (a secondary alcohol); only butanal reduces Tollens' reagent, because the hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon allows easy oxidation to butanoic acid, whereas a ketone can be oxidised only by strong oxidising agents at high temperature, with cleavage of a C–C bond to give a mixture of carboxylic acids with fewer carbon atoms
B) NaBH₄ reduces both to butane; both reduce Tollens' reagent
C) Butanone reduces Tollens' reagent, because its carbonyl carbon carries two alkyl groups; butanal does not
D) Ketones are oxidised more easily than aldehydes, and mild oxidation of butanone gives butanoic acid without loss of carbon
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Butanal → butan-1-ol, butanone → butan-2-ol; only the aldehyde gives Tollens' test; ketones need vigorous oxidation with C–C cleavage.
Concept: Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to primary and secondary alcohols respectively by sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) or lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄), as well as by catalytic hydrogenation. Aldehydes differ from ketones in their oxidation reactions. Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids by common oxidising agents like nitric acid, potassium permanganate and potassium dichromate; even mild oxidising agents, mainly Tollens' reagent and Fehling's reagent, also oxidise aldehydes. Ketones are generally oxidised under vigorous conditions, that is, strong oxidising agents and elevated temperatures; their oxidation involves carbon–carbon bond cleavage to afford a mixture of carboxylic acids having fewer carbon atoms than the parent ketone. On warming an aldehyde with freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate solution (Tollens' reagent), a bright silver mirror is produced due to the formation of silver metal.
Why: Oxidising an aldehyde only replaces the C–H of the CHO group by C–OH; oxidising a ketone requires breaking a C–C bond, which needs much more energy.
Why not the others: (B) NaBH₄ reduces C=O to CH–OH, not to CH₂; ketones do not reduce Tollens' reagent. (C) It is the aldehyde that reduces Tollens' reagent. (D) Ketones are harder to oxidise, and their oxidation breaks C–C bonds.
Key point: Aldehyde → 1° alcohol, ketone → 2° alcohol on reduction; aldehydes are oxidised easily (Tollens'), ketones only with C–C cleavage.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the acid strengths of acetic and chloroacetic acids from pKa values, the ratio of degrees of ionisation at equal concentration, and the effect of more and of more electronegative halogens
questions.question: pKa values: CH₃COOH 4.76, ClCH₂COOH 2.86, Cl₂CHCOOH 1.29, Cl₃CCOOH 0.70, FCH₂COOH 2.59. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Acetic acid is about 1.9 times stronger than chloroacetic acid

B) Ka(ClCH₂COOH)/Ka(CH₃COOH) = 10^1.90 ≈ 79, so at the same (dilute) concentration chloroacetic acid is ionised about √79 ≈ 9 times as much; acidity increases with the number of chlorine atoms (Cl₃C– > Cl₂CH– > ClCH₂– > CH₃–), and fluoroacetic acid is stronger than chloroacetic acid because F is more electronegative
C) The Ka ratio is 79, and the degrees of ionisation are also in the ratio 79 : 1
D) Chlorine atoms are electron-releasing, so trichloroacetic acid is the weakest acid in the list
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ka ratio ≈ 79; ionisation ratio ≈ 9; acidity rises with number and electronegativity of halogens.
Concept: Electron-withdrawing groups increase the acidity of carboxylic acids by stabilising the conjugate base through delocalisation of the negative charge by inductive and/or resonance effects; conversely, electron-donating groups decrease the acidity by destabilising the conjugate base. The effect of the following groups in increasing acidity follows the order Ph < I < Br < Cl < F < CN < NO₂ < CF₃. Thus chloroacetic acid is more acidic than acetic acid, and di- and trichloroacetic acids are progressively stronger.
Given: pKa(CH₃COOH) = 4.76; pKa(ClCH₂COOH) = 2.86.
Formula/Principle: Ka = 10^(−pKa); for a weak acid at concentration c, α ≈ √(Ka/c).
Step 1: Ka ratio = 10^(4.76 − 2.86) = 10^1.90 ≈ 79.
Step 2: At equal c, α₁/α₂ = √(Ka₁/Ka₂) = √79 ≈ 8.9.
Step 3: pKa decreases (acid strength increases) along CH₃COOH (4.76) > ClCH₂COOH (2.86) > Cl₂CHCOOH (1.29) > Cl₃CCOOH (0.70); FCH₂COOH (2.59) < ClCH₂COOH.
Why: Each halogen pulls electron density away from the carboxylate group by the –I effect, spreading the negative charge and stabilising the anion; more halogens or a more electronegative halogen stabilise it further.
Why not the others: (A) Chloroacetic acid is the stronger acid, and a pKa difference of 1.90 is a factor of 79 in Ka. (C) α varies as the square root of Ka. (D) Halogens are electron-withdrawing; trichloroacetic acid is the strongest here.
Key point: ΔpKa = 1 ⇒ Ka changes 10-fold; α ∝ √Ka at fixed concentration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using the Heisenberg uncertainty principle to compare the minimum velocity uncertainty of an electron in an atom with that of a small ball, and the de Broglie wavelength of the ball
questions.question: Taking h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, compare (i) an electron whose position is known to within 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (about the size of an atom) with (ii) a 10 g ball whose position is known to within 1.0 mm. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Both have Δv of about 10⁻³⁰ m s⁻¹, so the uncertainty principle is unimportant for both
B) The electron has Δv ≥ 5.8 × 10⁻³⁰ m s⁻¹ and the ball 5.3 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹
C) The electron has Δv ≥ 5.8 m s⁻¹; the ball's de Broglie wavelength at 10 m s⁻¹ is 6.6 × 10⁻³⁵ m

D) The electron has Δv ≥ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, comparable with electron speeds in atoms, so a definite trajectory (Bohr orbit) is meaningless; the ball has Δv ≥ 5.3 × 10⁻³⁰ m s⁻¹, utterly negligible; moving at 10 m s⁻¹ the ball has de Broglie wavelength 6.6 × 10⁻³³ m, far too small to detect
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Electron Δv ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; ball Δv ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻³⁰ m s⁻¹; ball λ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³³ m.
Concept: Werner Heisenberg stated the uncertainty principle: it is impossible to determine simultaneously the exact position and exact momentum (or velocity) of an electron, Δx × Δp ≥ h/4π. One of the important implications is that it rules out the existence of definite paths or trajectories of electrons and other similar particles. The effect of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle is significant only for the motion of microscopic objects and is negligible for macroscopic objects. de Broglie proposed that matter, like radiation, should exhibit dual behaviour, with λ = h/mv.
Given: h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; electron m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, Δx = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; ball m = 1.0 × 10⁻² kg, Δx = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m.
Formula/Principle: Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx); λ = h/(mv).
Step 1: Electron: Δv ≥ 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴/(4π × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴/1.145 × 10⁻³⁹ ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
Step 2: Ball: Δv ≥ 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴/(4π × 1.0 × 10⁻² × 1.0 × 10⁻³) = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴/1.257 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻³⁰ m s⁻¹.
Step 3: Ball λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴/(1.0 × 10⁻² × 10) = 6.6 × 10⁻³³ m.
Why: Because of the tiny mass of the electron, confining it to atomic dimensions forces a velocity uncertainty as large as the velocity itself; for an everyday object the same principle gives an immeasurably small uncertainty.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) The two values are interchanged or wrongly equal. (C) Δv for the electron is off by 10⁵, and λ is off by a factor of 100.
Key point: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π matters only for microscopic particles; it removes the idea of fixed electron orbits.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Volumes of hydrogen released by equal masses of sodium and potassium with water, and trends in reactivity, hydration enthalpy and ionic mobility in group 1
questions.question: 1.00 g of sodium and 1.00 g of potassium are separately added to excess water (Na = 23, K = 39; molar volume 22.4 L at STP). Which statement is correct?
options: A) Both give 0.487 L of H₂ at STP; lithium reacts most vigorously; Li⁺(aq) has the highest mobility

B) Na gives 0.487 L and K 0.287 L of H₂ at STP; K reacts more vigorously than Na (reactivity with water increases down the group, Li being least vigorous despite its most negative E°); the magnitude of hydration enthalpy decreases Li⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺, so Li⁺, the most heavily hydrated, has the lowest ionic mobility in water
C) Na gives 0.974 L and K 0.574 L of H₂; hydration enthalpy increases down the group
D) Na gives 0.287 L and K 0.487 L; Li⁺(aq) moves fastest because it is the smallest bare ion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Na: 0.487 L, K: 0.287 L; K is more reactive; Li⁺ is most hydrated and least mobile.
Concept: The alkali metals react with water to form hydroxide and dihydrogen: 2M + 2H₂O → 2M⁺ + 2OH⁻ + H₂. Although lithium has the most negative E° value, its reaction with water is less vigorous than that of sodium, which has the least negative E° value among the alkali metals; this behaviour of lithium is attributed to its small size and very high hydration energy. The hydration enthalpies of alkali metal ions decrease with increase in ionic sizes: Li⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺ > Rb⁺ > Cs⁺. Li⁺ has the maximum degree of hydration, and for this reason lithium salts are mostly hydrated; the larger hydrated ion moves more slowly in solution.
Given: m = 1.00 g each; M(Na) = 23, M(K) = 39 g mol⁻¹; 22.4 L mol⁻¹ at STP.
Formula/Principle: 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂ ⇒ n(H₂) = n(M)/2.
Step 1: n(Na) = 1.00/23 = 0.0435 mol ⇒ n(H₂) = 0.0217 mol ⇒ V = 0.0217 × 22.4 = 0.487 L.
Step 2: n(K) = 1.00/39 = 0.0256 mol ⇒ n(H₂) = 0.0128 mol ⇒ V = 0.287 L.
Step 3: Equal masses give less H₂ from the heavier metal, though potassium reacts much more violently.
Why: Each metal atom gives one electron, so H₂ produced depends on moles of metal; the vigour of the reaction depends on kinetics (low ionisation enthalpy, low melting point), not on the yield.
Why not the others: (A) Equal masses are not equal moles; Li is least vigorous, and Li⁺(aq) is least mobile. (C) Doubles the H₂, and hydration enthalpy decreases down the group. (D) Values swapped; Li⁺(aq) is the largest hydrated ion.
Key point: n(H₂) = ½ n(M); reactivity with water rises down group 1; hydration enthalpy and hydrated size fall down the group.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading Born–Haber data for MgO to calculate its lattice enthalpy and explaining why it forms despite the endothermic second electron gain and second ionisation
questions.question: For MgO (all in kJ mol⁻¹): enthalpy of sublimation of Mg = +148; first and second ionisation enthalpies of Mg = +738 and +1451; ½ bond dissociation enthalpy of O₂ = +249; first and second electron gain enthalpies of O = −141 and +798; enthalpy of formation of MgO(s) = −602. What is the lattice enthalpy of MgO (energy to separate one mole of solid into gaseous ions), and what does it show?
options: A) +602 kJ mol⁻¹; the formation of MgO is endothermic
B) +3243 kJ mol⁻¹; the second electron gain releases energy
C) −3845 kJ mol⁻¹; MgO cannot be formed from its elements

D) +3845 kJ mol⁻¹; although forming gaseous Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ from the elements needs +3243 kJ mol⁻¹ (including the endothermic IE₂ and second electron gain), the very large lattice enthalpy, due to the doubly charged small ions, makes the overall formation exothermic (−602 kJ mol⁻¹); it is nearly five times that of NaCl (+788 kJ mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Lattice enthalpy = +3845 kJ mol⁻¹; its size overcomes +3243 kJ mol⁻¹ needed to make the gaseous ions.
Concept: The lattice enthalpy of an ionic solid is defined as the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into gaseous constituent ions. It is not possible to determine lattice enthalpy directly by experiment, so an indirect method is used, constructing an enthalpy diagram called a Born–Haber cycle, based on Hess's law. Ionic bonds are favoured by low ionisation enthalpy, a large negative electron gain enthalpy and, above all, a large lattice enthalpy; the stability of an ionic compound is provided by the energy released in the formation of the crystal lattice.
Given: ΔsubH = 148; IE₁ = 738; IE₂ = 1451; ½D(O=O) = 249; Δeg₁ = −141; Δeg₂ = +798; ΔfH = −602 (kJ mol⁻¹).
Formula/Principle: Hess's law: ΔfH = ΔsubH + IE₁ + IE₂ + ½D + Δeg₁ + Δeg₂ − ΔlatticeH (lattice enthalpy defined as positive for separation).
Step 1: Energy to form gaseous ions: 148 + 738 + 1451 + 249 − 141 + 798 = +3243 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: −602 = 3243 − ΔlatticeH ⇒ ΔlatticeH = 3243 + 602 = +3845 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 3: Ratio to NaCl: 3845/788 ≈ 4.9.
Why: Lattice energy grows with the product of the ionic charges and falls with ionic separation; Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are small and doubly charged, giving a lattice energy large enough to pay for both endothermic steps.
Why not the others: (A) Confuses ΔfH with lattice enthalpy; formation is exothermic. (B) That is only the cost of making the ions; the second electron gain is endothermic. (C) Sign convention wrong, and MgO is readily formed.
Key point: Born–Haber: ΔfH = (cost of gaseous ions) − lattice enthalpy; high charges give very large lattice enthalpies.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating formal charges in H₃O⁺, BF₄⁻, CN⁻ and two Lewis structures of SO₄²⁻, and using formal charges to choose the preferred structure
questions.question: Formal charge = (valence electrons) − (non-bonding electrons) − ½(bonding electrons). Which statement is correct?
options: A) O in H₃O⁺ is +1; B in BF₄⁻ is −1; in CN⁻, C is −1 and N is 0; in SO₄²⁻, the structure with four S–O single bonds gives S +2 and each O −1, whereas the structure with two S=O and two S–O bonds gives S 0, the double-bonded O 0 and the single-bonded O −1; the second is preferred because it has the smaller formal charges, and in both the formal charges add up to −2
B) O in H₃O⁺ is 0; B in BF₄⁻ is +1; in CN⁻ the charge is on N
C) Formal charges are the real charges on the atoms; S in SO₄²⁻ always carries +6
